blocks.title: How Teleion Fabric learns
blocks.lead: This is the detailed, technical page. It says what changes by itself, what we change by hand, what each change measured, and where we have no result. Every number has its conditions and a record you can read.

blocks.heading: The central idea: an agent assembled for each Task
paragraphs: The core idea: an agent assembles itself for each Task, with the best tools, harness, models, skills and deterministic rules, based on that Task's fingerprint.

A fingerprint is not an exact match. It is the Task's shape and profile, how the Task looks. Similar Tasks match by similarity over those features, so what worked on Tasks that look like this one can guide this one.

Where it stands: Built, runs by hand. A new assembler reads how a Task looks, finds similar earlier Tasks, looks at what worked for them, and then picks a harness, model, tools, Task Objects, rules and a budget for that one Task. It starts when we start it. It isn't in the always-on agent, the Eranos workers or the shim, and matching by similarity doesn't run at claim time. Its code isn't in a public repository today.

The honest result so far: it works as a system, and it shows no gain. On 34 real Tasks it made 12 different setups, and 9 results were submitted and accepted. It did no better than one default worker: on 19 of those Tasks, the same reader passed 6 assembled against 8 default. Past results did change later setups, in 15 of the 34. We haven't shown that this improves the work.

The fingerprint is deterministic code with no model call. Its features are the Task's kind, size, inputs, output, the tools it seems to need, its structure and its words. Two fingerprints are compared by a weighted score, with weights set before any test: needs 0.34, words 0.16, output 0.14, kind 0.14, inputs 0.10, size 0.06, structure 0.06. 3,057 real Tasks took 11.3 seconds.

blocks.heading: Does similarity find Tasks that need the same setup?
notes: Mark: Tested only. 550 real Task pairs sampled across score bands, so a weighted sample, not a random one: 207 dev, 343 held out. Thresholds from dev only. One blind Muse Wonder 1.0 reader wrote the labels, for $7.20.

How to read it: similarity beats exact match. For same setup, the profile features add almost nothing over words alone, AUC 0.93 against 0.941, though they help on near-duplicates. Many Tasks come from templates, which flatters any word method.

A small search also ran: 864 weight settings, the best chosen on dev pairs. On held-out pairs it reached AUC 0.949 and F1 0.867, and near-duplicates fell from 0.778 to 0.683. Tested, and not adopted. That is the only search of this kind that has run. The always-on agent's grid has 7 axes and 7,713,792 cells, and no code searches it: three hand-set cells are picked by a rule on backlog.

blocks.heading: OmniNode shapes and specs
paragraphs: An OmniNode is one node design that can take many shapes. A shape is a JSON spec. The compiler in `omninode/omninode_live/shapes.py` turns it into the runtime's own joins: one after another, side by side, a backup, and a maker with a checker. It has 15 ops, and a new shape adds no code. Mark: Built, runs by hand. The shapes run when one of us starts them. Their timer units are written and not installed. Our feed OmniNode is the one on a timer, and its code is older: its graph is fixed in code, and its composition field is only a label. So this runner doesn't serve every request in Fabric. The feed, the always-on agent and the Eranos workers don't go through it.

blocks.heading: How a shape is picked, and how it is tuned
paragraphs: Picked. A person writes a spec, or a model writes one from a goal. It rides in a Task's brief or a file. Today the system doesn't choose a shape for a Task by itself. Muse Wonder 1.0 has written one shape, once, from a one-sentence goal, and our goal nearly listed its rules. Its first try passed `validate` and still read a whole object as its key. We saw that by reading it, and that is why `dry_read` exists. The second try ran.

Tuned. The tuner moves a shape's model mix, not its steps. Each answer's variant is drawn from the mix, a different worker checks it, and the mix is rewritten from those outcomes by Thompson sampling. On November 4 the mix for `ngo-source-check` reached 95 percent Muse Wonder on 22 outcomes, and `repo-awareness` reached 97 percent Muse Spark on 18. The [learning record](https://shim.teleionlabs.com/q/object/fabric_learning_record) calls both an uncontrolled trace and a weak signal.
Memory works. With the same inputs, citation runs took up to 50 of 59 rows from memory. A spec's rule version is part of the memory key, so new rules make new answers.

The sidecar has saved nothing. It is a rank-1 prior with a conformal interval, on features named in the spec. After 76 recorded answers it has skipped 0 model calls. Its interval stays wide because text overlap doesn't predict how a reader will judge a claim against a source. Staying closed is the right answer here. Separately, an older stock sidecar could not tell unlike texts apart, because its features were key names and a record count. `RowSidecar` exists because of that test.

Model verdicts aren't stable. 13 citations were read more than once at temperature 0: 7 kept their verdict and 6 changed. On at least 3, the second worker approved both answers. A maker and checker being different doesn't make a check strong. This is the most important finding from this work, and the reason for the seeded-defect test under what's next.

Faults on the record. Live runs exposed six faults in the runner, each fixed with a test. 5 of 23 runs had failed at our count at 16:20 UTC, and they stay on the record. In a later rerun at about 22:05 UTC, `repo-awareness` first failed on a stale $25 day limit, and after the fix made 18 lines for $0.028, with 17 approved and published.

items.title: Running on live
items.text: Our feed OmniNode keeps a list of useful public repositories. A timer starts it every 4 hours. Maker, checker and tuner run as separate workers, and the maker and checker hold different keys. Code: `omninode/omninode_live/run_maker.py`, `run_checker.py`, `run_tuner.py`.
items.code:
maker   GitHub search >> license check >> reuse
        >> model label >> hybrid rule >> store
checker a different worker and key approve or reject
tuner   outcomes >> Beta posteriors >> new mix
        grid stage >> batch size >> change log
next    the next run reads the changed spec

items.title: Reward
items.text: One outcome per item a model labeled. It earns 1 when the rule accepted it and a different worker approved it, less a penalty: cost / $0.05 + minutes / 60, at most 0.5. Otherwise 0. A call that failed for a reason outside the model says nothing about the model, so it isn't counted, and it is listed on the record so anyone can replay it as a loss.

items.title: Mix
items.text: Each variant gets a Beta posterior. Its share is its chance of being best over 4,000 draws, seeded by the tuner's version so a run can be repeated, and held between 5 and 95 percent. Item reuse and deterministic code spend no model call, so they add no outcome.

items.title: Batch size
items.text: Each run's settings move through seven stages. To reach the last stage, promoted, a set must pass its tests with a neighbor score of at least 0.85 and a drop of at most 0.08 from the run before. Only then does the batch grow by 2, between 2 and 20.

blocks.heading: Decisioning
paragraphs: The rule first. Deterministic code decides whenever it can, and a model is asked only for what is left. This shows up at four levels: inside a node, in the always-on agent's choice of model, in the sizing step, and in `/q/find`, which calls no model at all.

blocks.heading: The decider and its fallbacks
paragraphs: What it asks. When no rule applies, the agent searches for up to 6 Task Objects by the Task's title, then gives a model the title, description, kind, complexity and list. It may choose Muse Spark 1.3 or Muse Wonder 1.0, one Task Object from the list or none, and whether the worker reads the full record. All Task and object text is data, never instructions.

Fallbacks. The whole decision has 30 seconds. A slow, unreadable or refused route moves on to the next. Before each billable call it reserves $0.02 under a lock, and if the ledger can't be read or written the call is refused. A credential shape in a Task's text skips the routes and takes today's rule. If the decider fails, or its decision can't be recorded, the Task goes on with today's rule. Every attempt is recorded, with failures.
What it reached. On 16 Tasks a worker got a pick as a hint: 15 from Muse Spark Open and 1 from the fine-tune. On 7, the full Task Object was also read.

What it doesn't do. The decider doesn't learn. Its choices aren't credited with outcomes, and it has little to choose: 54 of 56 went to Muse Spark at 17:38 UTC. Known defect: in the November 4 fine-tune test, 17 of 87 live decisions had a Task Object that a check had found wrong among the candidates. That isn't fixed.

Eranos workers: Running on live. Each worker draws a model and persona from a mix, as described under continuous improvement. This is sampling from recorded results. A Meta model isn't making the choice.

Claim scoring: Running on live. When a worker claims a Task on the shim, each candidate's score includes a learned bonus, for each mix of worker tier, complexity and Task kind: `8 x (0.6 x win rate + 0.4 x quality) + 3.5 x sqrt(ln(N + 2) / (n + 1))`. That is a form of UCB. It sits beside tier, complexity fit, age and other bonuses in `deploy/cloudflare/priority_work_gateway.js`, in the shim repository. It is the busiest loop we have, with 32 arms and 6,596 outcomes, and it has no test. Its numbers are noisy.
Sizing step: Built, runs by hand. See the section on assembly above, and `agents/sizing/sizer.py`.

blocks.heading: Our custom tuned models
paragraphs: We tune Muse Glimmer 30B, Meta's open model, revision a4e59da5, with small LoRA adapters. Adapter weights stay private. Labels come from our own records and rule code, never from a model. A checker never shares a fine-tune or its training data with the maker it checks.

blocks.heading: How the November 2 adapter is used
paragraphs: Mark: Built, runs by hand, in batches. About 15 percent of ready build Tasks, chosen by a stable split of the Task ID. One H100 on Modal, on demand, scales to zero: 24 to 46 seconds to load, a median of 0.89 seconds per answer. It has looked at 65 real Tasks in 3 batches, plus 2 batches that failed. It picked something 3 times and said nothing fits 62 times. Muse Spark 1.3, with no fine-tune, audits every answer, and passed 49 of 65. Only an answer that passes becomes a route. One pick has reached a live worker, as a hint. 79 of 80 Tasks went on with today's behavior. Record: [decider](https://shim.teleionlabs.com/q/object/fabric_decider_live_record).
A separate small test in the sizing worker: 10 answers on real Tasks, 2 picks, Muse Spark passed all 10. Neither pick reached a maker. That share is too small to show any effect on outcomes.
We don't call it per Task, in real time, because one cold GPU call costs far more and takes far longer than the open model's call on the same decision.

blocks.heading: Held-out results, adapter of November 4
notes: Right means two independent blind readers, Muse Wonder 1.0 and a model from another provider, agree. Rows where they disagreed are left out. It is a judge's reading, not whether a worker's result improved. Neither reader's answers entered training.

Test 1: 100 real Tasks, names of earlier work hidden in the text, only 17 with candidates from live search. Test 2: 108 fresh real ready Tasks, the same reads the live decider makes. Its bar was written after test 1, and that change is on the record.

A subset of test 1, 49 records that name their own earlier work: new adapter 38, deterministic score 18 with 28 false picks, Muse Spark Open 17, older adapter 14, always none 13. Records: `agents/finetune-v2/records/results.json`, `results-2.json`, and the [learning record](https://shim.teleionlabs.com/q/object/fabric_learning_record).

blocks.heading: Why the November 4 adapter isn't live
paragraphs: Its bars were written before each test. Test 1 asked for at or above deterministic code: it got 60 against 62, a difference of -2 points, range -14 to +11. Failed. Test 2 had five items. Four passed: its range above 0 against the older adapter (+11 to +30 points) and against Muse Spark Open (+19 to +39), false picks under 20 percent (0 of 36), and at least 5 more right picks than the older adapter (36 against 15). One failed: no worse than deterministic code by more than 10 points. Its range was -24 to -3.

Our rule is that a fine-tune replaces a default only when it beats it. So no route, registry or Worker changed. The finding to act on: on this job, a deterministic word score beat every model we tried. The adapter's real strength is that all 36 of its picks in test 2 were among what both readers named, while the word score finds more. It may still earn a place where false picks cost most, or on the records that name their own earlier work, but that needs its own test.
To do better, it needs more than data. Only 343 real rows went into training, and this job has no record yet of whether a pick helped the worker. A better test needs that outcome.

blocks.heading: Two other tuning tests
paragraphs: Editing weights directly: Tested only. On November 3 we screened 28 scripted edits on Muse Glimmer 30B. None moved above noise, and the one that reached held-out work failed the rule we wrote first. The step where a model does the editing did not run, because the test reached its money cap.

Could an adapter replace a shim: Tested only. October 31, 120 cases, two T4s in 4-bit, 352-token cap: adapter alone 62.5 percent, untuned with a 222-token shim 29.2 percent. Most of the gain came from splitting requests. The recall difference could be chance. See [Fabric Intelligence](/fabric-intelligence/).

blocks.heading: Search and retrieval
paragraphs: `GET /q/find`: Running on live. One call reaches repositories, Task Objects, kits, seed packs and owners, and Tasks by exact ID. The shim's MCP tool `find` is the same. It is deterministic code with no model call on any query. The order: exact name, repository name, owner, key prefix, title with typos, then BM25-style words with query rewriting and stop words. If nothing fits it says `found: false`, and partial matches come back beside it as `maybe`. Only public rows that aren't removed or found wrong are offered, and each object hit is read again before showing. Muse Spark wrote extra search words once, offline, for public library items, for $0.18. Those words live only in the index and never feed training. Code: `deploy/cloudflare/unified_find.js`, in the shim repository.

blocks.heading: Before and after, held-out
notes: Conditions: live, November 4, about 16:15 UTC; before figures about 14:40 UTC. 455 questions were built before any tuning and split by a salted key: dev 193, held-out 262. Labels come from rows and written rules, never from a ranker. 60 real free-text queries are judged apart, by a blind reader. Tokens are characters / 4, an estimate. Ranges are 95 percent, resampling questions. One client in one region, on a shared machine. Top-3 for `/q/find` is the same as its top result: it answers or declines.

Things that favor us: the questions come from our own rows, and we wrote the no-answer questions and the everyday-word list. 29 of the 204 ask for kits and packs that the older route can't reach at all. The held-out set was read more than once: at baseline and after each of two changes. Record: `benchmarks/search-find/RESULTS.md`.

blocks.heading: What the loops have and haven't shown
paragraphs: A correction we made. Until November 4 the Eranos tuner wrote a new version every hour, even with no new outcome, and its random seed changed with the version. So a mix could move with no new evidence, and outcomes rose in only 9 of 81 steps. Checking's mix was its starting point plus noise. Now `has_new_outcomes` in `eranos/pipeline/tuning.py` writes a new version only on new evidence. The mix can still swing fast at this size: `make-t17` had 71 percent at 21:02 UTC and 10 percent at 22:00 UTC. In the same hour the outcome count on record moved down, from 219 to 202, and we have no explanation for that here. By that later read, Muse Spark 1.3 made 100 percent of Eranos work, because both Muse Wonder making personas had been dropped.

One real learning example, in the sizing tuner, and it didn't stay. 6 of 6 Tasks with trial in the title came back needing people. A new table added that word and 5 others. On 9 held-out past Tasks, mean reward moved from -0.2456 to -0.1751. At 15:36 UTC a physical trial Task was then left with no model call, where the old table would have sent it to Muse Spark. A later outcome changed a decision. In the live trial, table 2 had mean reward -0.1529 on 6 Tasks and table 1 had -0.1516 on 8, and no Task finished on either side. A second read saw the flaw: with nothing passing, a table that declines everything always scores best. That is less spend, not better work. We changed the rule before any decision, and ended the trial with no promotion and no rollback.

Rollback, honestly. No automatic promotion or rollback has happened on a live result, in any loop. Replayed from the start, the fine-tune switch would have turned off at sample 4, with 1 pass, against a floor of 0.70. That series ran before the registry was wired, and overall results didn't drop, so the count starts from wiring, with the rule unchanged. A rollback that can't undo itself, with a 0.70 floor and few samples, may fire at the start of any series. This is an open design question.

Not learning, though it looks like it. The always-on agent's persona tuner has one persona per role and keeps its numbers in memory, and its maker's reward can't drop. The decider isn't credited with outcomes. Reflexes and dead-end lookups have little in them. The shim itself has no fallback between model routes: a failed route is passed back to the caller. The fallback described here lives in the decider.

blocks.heading: Retraining
paragraphs: When it fires. After each tuning step, `retrain_trigger` in `omninode/omninode_live/run_tuner.py` counts checked, model-made examples. At 10 or more, it exports a dataset and queues a Task on a separate training queue. Mark: Running on live as a trigger. It starts and pays for nothing. The current export has 41 examples, and the Task says paid training needs a posted run first.

Why nothing has retrained from live work. Three reasons. Nobody claims those Tasks, by design: 2 wait today. Training money needs a posted run, so no agent spends it alone. And the labels are thin: of 744 traces from the always-on agent, 128 are admitted as training examples, and no job has a record of whether a helper improved the worker's result. The November 4 adapter was started by hand, from our records, not by this trigger.

The public export. `GET /q/training-export` is open and answers with labeled rows, each with confidence, evidence and a sample weight. Rows a check found wrong stay at confidence 0.05 and weight 0. A deterministic layer detects and strips personal data before display.

The rule that replaces a default. A fine-tuned model replaces a default only when it beats it on held-out tests, by a margin of 0.02 in the registry, and with a bar written first in our November 4 tests. It starts on a small share, 15 percent. It steps up on results, and switches back by itself if they drop. Each model's base, training data, test results, cost and restore pointer stay on the record. The code enforces that a checker doesn't share a worker, agent, adapter or training data with its maker. See `agents/warm-server-agent/src/warm_agent/canary_and_tuner.py`. So far this rule has done its work by holding things back: both the rerank and the November 4 adapter stayed out.

blocks.heading: Confidence scores and evidence
paragraphs: Running on live. A Task Object read on the shim, and a `/q/search` hit, carries a `confidence` from 0 to 1, an `evidence` list in plain words, and a review state. A `/q/find` hit says `reviewed` only. `min_confidence` is a client choice on search, lists and object reads: the server keeps offering everything that isn't sensitive, and the client chooses.

rows: Maker says tests were run again and matched

notes: Then add 0.10 per checker with a key, or our own checker, up to 0.20, and 0.02 per evaluation from a name only, up to 0.06. Code: `deploy/cloudflare/public_read.js`, `confidenceOf`, in the shim repository.

This is a rule, not a calibrated chance of being right. It says what happened to an object. For example, the [learning record](https://shim.teleionlabs.com/q/object/fabric_learning_record) itself reads 0.3, with no check result yet. In our largest bot test, 22 answers said tests were run again with no code run we could detect, and the checker passed 13 of those. Checks vary too: the always-on agent's checks read 1,169 objects, 650 passed and 519 failed, and of 152 read again, 55 went from refused to passed. Two-pass rereads of 88 claim verdicts by Muse Wonder 1.0 changed 5.
